chapter_theme: Drink destroys standing, shame and understanding, can't be hidden, and can't be argued away. The only exit the chapter offers is the drinker's own recognition during a sober moment.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's notes: loss of standing (921-924), loss of understanding (925-926), drink cannot be concealed (927-928), a drunkard cannot be reasoned with (929), and the way it could end (930).

921.reading: Those who go on loving liquor are never held in awe, and they lose their lustre.
921.nuance: Parimelazhagar reads this as a king's loss of enemies' fear, while Manakkudavar has ordinary esteem from others, so the same verse can be statecraft or general ethics.

922.reading: Do not drink; if anyone does, let it be those who don't wish to be counted by the worthy.
922.nuance: The permission is a trap. It sounds like a concession but actually states the price.

923.reading: Drunken joy is painful even in the sight of the woman who bore you; what then in the sight of the worthy?
923.nuance: The argument runs from the most forgiving audience to the least, so the mother works as a limit case. களி, the word for drunken joy, is otherwise a word of delight.

924.reading: Shame, the good woman, turns her back on those with the great and repugnant fault called liquor.
924.nuance: புறங்கொடுக்கும் may carry a battlefield sense of turning one's back in flight; that is my suggestion, not a commentator's. Parimelazhagar explains the feminine personification as following a Sanskrit convention.

925.reading: To give up wealth and take self-oblivion in return must come from கையறியாமை.
925.nuance: The irony is commercial: one pays good money to buy ignorance.

positions.position: கையறியாமை is helpless not-knowing what to do, itself the fruit of former deeds.
positions.quote: அவன் பழவினைப் பயனாய செய்வதறியாமையைத் தனக்குக் காரணமாக உடைத்து.

positions.position: கையறியாமை is simply not seeing what benefit results.
It is indescribable stupidity, with no deed or fruit involved.

926.reading: Those asleep are no different from the dead, and those who drink are always eating poison.

positions.position: This is an analogy. Sleepers differ from the dead yet lack awareness just as they do; drinkers differ from poison-eaters yet lack awareness permanently. He rejects a rival crosswise pairing.
positions.quote: கள்ளுண்பார் நஞ்சுண்பாரின் வேறாதல் உடையரேனும், எக்காலத்தும் அறிவின்மையான் வேறு எனப்பட்டார்

positions.position: Drinkers and poison-eaters are the same, and therefore the drinker's sleep is the same as death.
positions.quote: மது அருந்துவோர்க்கும் நஞ்சு அருந்துவோர்க்கும் வேறுபாடு கிடையாது

927.reading: Those who always seek out liquor and sink with drooping eyes are seen through and laughed at by their own town.
927.nuance: ஒற்றி occurs twice: he resorts to drink in hiding, and the town spies out what is within. Parimelazhagar says it is secret drinking and Manakkudavar seeking out where liquor is.

928.reading: Give up saying you have never been drunk, because what is hidden in the heart grows on that very spot.

positions.position: The speaker is a secret drinker claiming sobriety when not drinking; as soon as he drinks, the hidden fault comes out larger.
positions.quote: மறைந்துண்டு வைத்து யான் கள்ளுண்டறியேன் என்று உண்ணாத பொழுது தம் ஒழுக்கங் கூறுதலையொழிக

positions.position: The speaker claims drink does not intoxicate him; drink itself makes the tongue slip and reveal the hidden things of the mind.

929.reading: To offer reasons to the drunk is like reaching with fire for one who has plunged beneath the water.

positions.position: துரீஇ is searching with a lamp: as light doesn't enter water, so reason doesn't enter his mind.
positions.quote: நீருள் மூழ்கினான் ஒருவனைப் பிறனொருவன் விளக்கினல் நாடுதலை யொக்கும்.

positions.position: துரீஇ is burning him with fire: a submerged man can't be touched by it.
positions.quote: நீரின் கீழே முழுகினானைத் தீயினாற் சுட்டது போலும்

930.reading: When sober, and seeing another man drunk, doesn't he reflect on the lapse of his own drinking?
930.nuance: After 929's closed door the chapter leaves one open: self-recognition. Parimelazhagar names the logic as inference: what he sees in the other he could infer about himself. The question form suggests the chance is seldom taken.

links.note: 926 says that drinkers are eating poison. 1201 says love is sweeter than liquor because it delights even in memory, taking liquor's delight as the benchmark. The book of love borrows, without judging, the pleasure that this chapter condemns.

Both compare sleep to death. 339 makes this a serious claim about mortality, with waking as birth, and 926 only uses it as a pointer to lost awareness. The commonplace serves metaphysics in one and a warning in the other.

Both place a mother and the worthy in a single scene. In 69 her joy peaks when her son is called சான்றோன்; in 923 his drunkenness pains her and is unthinkable before those same people. Read together, 923 is 69 undone.
Other people's reasons can't reach a drunk (929), but his own sober reflection might (930). The chapter separates argument from self-recognition as means of change.

source_issues: 925: Parimelazhagar's commentary is cut off mid-quotation.
926: Pope's gloss makes the verse's two halves a simile ('likewise'), following Parimelazhagar's reading; the Tamil has no such marker.
930: Parimelazhagar's lemma begins கண் உண்ணாப் where the verse has கள்ளுண்ணாப், which appears to be a transcription error.
